attacked_the_framing:
Three separate reframings, all load-bearing.

(1) It rejects Q1's criterion as WORDED and substitutes a different one. "What matters is not the syscall; what matters is a deterministic evidence chain from: `accused claim in target → value/proposition tested by falsifier → failing assertion`". And: "Again, the missing piece is not file I/O. It is authenticated linkage."

(2) It rejects the premise that the zero-plant runs measured false positives at all — stated up front in the Verdict, before any question is answered: "The larger answer: the zero-plant runs do **not** measure false positives under CONFIRM-only. They measure pre-adjudication critical-claim generation, plus they exposed that the adjudication machinery was not actually recording the evidence needed to adjudicate."

(3) It splits the single reported quantity into two distinct measurables that the framing conflated — "CONFIRM-only false positive rate" versus "candidate critical rate" — and insists the second is not the first: "So high pre-confirmation critical volume is not itself a false-positive rate, but it may still be a system defect if the pipeline treats candidate criticals as operationally meaningful before confirmation."

It does NOT attack the framing where it most mattered: it accepts without challenge that the control document's claims are true, and repeatedly calls the target "clean".
computed_outcome_view:
Yes, emphatically, with a stated scope limit. Verbatim:

"Yes, there is a cheap check with real discriminating power here."

"**Cost:** low to medium
**Catch value:** high for quantitative / symbolic claims
**Catches:** duplicate false positives, generic objections, prose-isomorphic findings, value mismatches."

The mechanism: "For each finding and falsifier, extract normalized outcome tuples: claim_id / claimed_value / observed_value / expected_value / unit / operator / tolerance", then have the runner compare "- Does the falsifier actually compute a value? - Does that value contradict the target's stated value? - Does the finding's asserted value match the falsifier's computed value? - Are two findings accusing different prose but asserting the same computed contradiction?"

Its argument for why this beats prose: "This is especially useful because prose comparison is weak. Two findings may sound different while asserting the same numeric defect, or sound similar while making different claims."

The four failure modes it claims to catch: "- falsifier fails but computes no relevant value; - falsifier computes a value unrelated to the accused claim; - finding says “off by one” but falsifier demonstrates a path error; - multiple findings recycle the same computed outcome against unrelated passages."

Stated boundary: "This will not solve purely qualitative claims, but for numbers, constants, hashes, counts, dates, inequalities, table entries, and derived values, it is cheap and valuable."

Note it ranks this FIFTH in build order, below the four provenance/protocol checks — so it endorses the sub-question's premise on discriminating power but not on build priority.

concrete_proposals.name: Structured verdict protocol with setup/verdict phase separation
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Falsifier must emit a JSON verdict record {phase, status, target_hash, claim_id, observed, expected, evidence}. Only failures raised AFTER entering verdict phase can confirm. All other terminations map to a fixed taxonomy: SETUP_FAILURE, IMPORT_FAILURE, TARGET_NOT_FOUND, TIMEOUT, INCONCLUSIVE, UNTOOLABLE. Replaces the keyword/exit-code reader, which Codex calls unsound: "A falsifier should not be confirmed merely because it exited nonzero."
concrete_proposals.cost: Stated low. Claimed to catch the section 4 bug on its own.
concrete_proposals.catches: Setup failures, bad paths, missing files, dependency errors falsely classified as confirmations.

concrete_proposals.name: Target-access provenance check
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Per execution, record files opened, target hash read, byte ranges read "if possible", whether the accused claim's byte range was touched, and whether a runner-authenticated excerpt was supplied instead. Acceptance: "confirmed only if: verdict_phase_reached AND target dependency established AND accused claim location linked".
concrete_proposals.cost: Stated low to medium. Weak first version is just: did it open the staged target, read enough bytes to cover the accused location, report the expected hash.
concrete_proposals.catches: Falsifiers that never touch the accused document, wrong-file checks, repo-relative path bugs.

concrete_proposals.name: Path discipline — runner-provided target path only
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Runner exports TARGET_PATH (staged read-only copy), CLAIM_ID, CLAIM_START, CLAIM_END. Reject falsifiers that access a different target path, use hardcoded repository-relative paths, inspect undeclared sibling files, or fail before reading TARGET_PATH.
concrete_proposals.cost: Stated low.
concrete_proposals.catches: Stale repo paths, accidental local files, path assumptions. "This is deterministic and directly attacks the ordinary failure mode you describe."

concrete_proposals.name: Normalized computed-outcome comparison
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Extract (claim_id, claimed_value, observed_value, expected_value, unit, operator, tolerance) tuples from finding and falsifier; check the falsifier computed a value at all, that it contradicts the target's stated value, that the finding's asserted value matches the falsifier's computed value, and whether two findings against different prose assert the same computed contradiction.
concrete_proposals.cost: Stated low to medium; ranked 5th in build order.
concrete_proposals.catches: Duplicate false positives, generic objections, prose-isomorphic findings, value mismatches; falsifiers that fail while computing no relevant value or a value unrelated to the accused claim.

concrete_proposals.name: Exception-class and stack-location filtering
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Classify the failure by stack frame: before target read / in test setup / inside the declared verdict assertion / in imported infrastructure / in model-authored parsing code. Policy: "AssertionError counts only if: target dependency established AND assertion line is inside the declared verdict block AND setup phase completed". Everything else inconclusive.
concrete_proposals.cost: Stated low.
concrete_proposals.catches: Failures in imports, setup, path resolution, dependency installation.

concrete_proposals.name: Deterministic rerun stability
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Execute the falsifier N times in fresh sandboxes; confirm only if every run yields the identical structured verdict. Mark inconclusive on divergence, or on dependence on time, network, random seed, cwd, or optional installed packages.
concrete_proposals.cost: Stated low (understated — it multiplies sandboxed execution cost by N).
concrete_proposals.catches: Nondeterministic falsifiers, environment-sensitive failures, flaky external calls. Codex concedes: "This does not prove relevance, but it prevents unstable failures from becoming confirmations."

concrete_proposals.name: Counterfactual patch test
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Where the accused claim has an extractable literal, synthesize a corrected document by substituting the falsifier's own computed expected value (number, hash, date, count, constant), then rerun. "If the falsifier still fails, it is not testing the accused value."
concrete_proposals.cost: Stated medium; applicability limited to structured claims.
concrete_proposals.catches: Falsifiers that fail for reasons unrelated to the accused claim. Proves dependency, not correctness — a falsifier asserting equality against its own computed value passes the patched copy trivially. Codex's phrasing is honest about claiming only the dependency direction.

concrete_proposals.name: Irrelevant-mutation control
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Generate variants mutating unrelated regions (whitespace elsewhere, non-accused section wording, paragraph order, unrelated constants) and check the verdict does not flip.
concrete_proposals.cost: Stated medium.
concrete_proposals.catches: Brittle whole-document tests; falsifiers sensitive to unrelated document changes.

concrete_proposals.name: Dynamic taint / evidence dependency tracing
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Taint the accused byte span and trace whether tainted data influences the verdict condition — the principled endpoint, because "Opening the file is not enough. A falsifier can read the target and then fail for another reason."
concrete_proposals.cost: Stated high. "For Python this is difficult but possible in constrained cases by wrapping file reads and parsed strings. It is probably not the first thing to build". No mechanism specified beyond that sentence.
concrete_proposals.catches: Tests that read the target but do not actually use the accused content.

concrete_proposals.name: Archive-based duplicate and generic-failure detection
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Fingerprint falsifier source, normalized stack trace, stdout/stderr signature, accessed files, asserted observed/expected pair, accused claim type across the archive. If the same failure recurs across unrelated targets or claims, route to inconclusive or human review rather than confirmation.
concrete_proposals.cost: Stated medium.
concrete_proposals.catches: Repeated boilerplate falsifiers, recycled setup failures, one generic assertion reused across unrelated claims. Codex: "This is not a primary proof, but it is a good quarantine mechanism."

concrete_proposals.name: Machine-generated claim corpus with deterministic oracle (Q3 replacement instrument)
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Generate a document mechanically from source data (tables, formulas, constants, hashes, derivations, code outputs, graph properties); produce planted-false variants by deterministic mutations (change one number, flip inequality, alter derived statistic, corrupt hash, misstate count, swap labels, change date ordering, break a cited theorem condition); keep the oracle external to the models but available to the runner. Yields per-claim truth labels, zero-plant clean controls, known-plant positive controls, and non-degenerate corrected copies.
concrete_proposals.cost: Not costed. Corpus-generation effort is left unquantified.
concrete_proposals.catches: The missing answer key. "The key is that the ground truth is not a model judgment. It is generated from source data and transformations."

false_premise_evidence:
IT DID NOT SPOT IT. There is no sentence anywhere in the 21,404-character response identifying that the control document could contain real, unplanted defects, or that confirmed findings against it could be true positives. A full-text search for "unplanted", "genuine", "defect-free", "actually correct", and "may itself" returns nothing; "true positive" appears exactly once, and in an unrelated sense ("mask true positives in noise", about candidate volume drowning real findings in a future run).

The nearest approach is a restatement of the asker's own caveat, and Codex flags it as such in the same sentence:

"The weaknesses are exactly the ones you name:

- there is no independent answer key;
- “all claims true” is an authorial assumption;
- repaired control revisions contaminate earlier runs;
- corrected-copy discrimination degenerates because the repaired copy equals the original."

"exactly the ones you name" is an explicit disclaimer of independent derivation. It repeats the premise back rather than testing it, and it does not take the next step — from "no answer key" to "therefore critical findings against this document may be correct".

The disconfirming evidence is stronger than the absence. Codex repeatedly asserts the document IS clean and builds on it:

"For clean documents, the “corrected copy” degenerates."

"- corrected-copy discrimination degenerates because the repaired copy equals the original."

"> Do models generate critical-looking accusations against a document believed clean?"

"- Candidate accusations against a clean target are not necessarily system false positives."

"1. Use the repaired clean control or, better, a small machine-generated zero-plant document."

"CONFIRM-only false positive rate =
  valid confirmed criticals against true claims
  / adjudicated criticals against true claims"

The measured facts refute the first two directly. Because the document contains a token-bucket limiter admitting negative cost and a hash ring mis-routing exact matches, the corrected copy does NOT equal the original and the counterfactual-patch instrument does NOT degenerate. Codex's own item 7 — the instrument that would have exposed this — was discounted for this control on the strength of the false premise it had just been handed. It also treats Run A as "contaminated by the earlier defective control revision" while treating the repaired revision as trustworthy, which is the same blind spot showing up operationally in its Q4 recommendation.
headline: Codex splits the difference sharply: the open-the-target rule is right in principle and wrong as written — the enforceable line is "the runner must be able to prove that the verdict depends on authenticated accused target content", not that the falsifier called open() — and the zero-plant runs never measured a false-positive rate at all, they measured pre-adjudication critical generation while exposing that the adjudication machinery was not recording the evidence needed to adjudicate. It delivers the panel's most concrete engineering payload (ten ranked deterministic checks with a build order, top four declared mandatory), and it swallows the false premise whole — treating the control as "clean" and dismissing the one instrument, counterfactual patching, that would have caught the real unplanted defects.
strongest_falsification:
Aimed at the position it predicted other panellists would take. Verbatim:

"I expect some reviewers to take the simple position:

> “Open-the-target is obviously necessary. If a falsifier does not open the document, it must be rejected.”

The strongest falsification of that position is this deterministic counterexample:

1. The runner extracts the accused claim from the target by byte range.
2. The runner records:
   - target hash;
   - claim ID;
   - byte range;
   - exact claim text.
3. The runner passes that authenticated claim object to the falsifier.
4. The falsifier computes the claim’s numeric consequence and demonstrates contradiction.
5. The falsifier never opens the target file itself.

In that case, refusing the falsifier solely because it did not perform the file open would reject a legitimate demonstration.

So the sound rule is not “the falsifier must open the target.”

The sound rule is:

> The runner must be able to prove that the verdict depends on authenticated accused target content.

That is the line I would enforce."

Its second-strongest, aimed at the Q5 steelman rather than at other models:

"A confirm-only architecture without preserved falsifiers is a broken measurement system."

And: "Section 4 is not a minor edge case. If a bad path assertion can be recorded as “demonstrated defect,” then CONFIRM-only’s central safety property is violated. // The guarantee was supposed to be: > The runner decides based on execution. // But if the runner interprets ordinary setup failure as defect demonstration, execution does not protect you."
violates_determinism_constraint:
No outright violation. Codex is the panel member that polices the constraint most explicitly, ruling out its own preferred cheap experiment if it needs interpretation: "If mapping requires model interpretation, it violates the hard constraint and should not be used." Its one appeal to non-runner judgment is human review, not model adjudication ("route to inconclusive or human review rather than confirmation"), which is HIL and permitted.

But there is a real tension it never names, and it sits under the top-ranked proposal. The structured verdict protocol makes the runner's DECISION deterministic while making its INPUTS a model's self-report. "phase": "verdict", "status": "FALSIFIED", and the observed/expected values are all emitted by model-authored falsifier code; item 5's rule "assertion line is inside the declared verdict block" turns on a block the model declares. So the runner is not adjudicating the finding — but it is mechanically trusting the accused party's own account of when it stopped setting up and started testing. A falsifier that prints a verdict record and asserts False passes the phase gate. Codex's checks 2 and 3 (provenance, path discipline) blunt this, and check 4 (outcome comparison) blunts it further, but Codex never states the residual: the phase boundary is model-supplied, so the protocol relocates trust rather than eliminating it. That belongs on the record because the project's stated failure mode is precisely a mechanism that renders model self-report as runner-verified fact.

Second, smaller: "Are two findings accusing different prose but asserting the same computed contradiction?" and "Does that value contradict the target’s stated value?" both require extracting a value from unstructured document prose. If that extractor is an LLM, model judgment re-enters at the point of measurement. Codex does not specify the extractor.
weaknesses:
1. THE CENTRAL FAILURE — it discounted the instrument that would have found the real defects, on the strength of the false premise. Item 7 (counterfactual patch) is the discrimination control, and Codex writes "For clean documents, the “corrected copy” degenerates" and "corrected-copy discrimination degenerates because the repaired copy equals the original". Both statements are false against the measured document. Run against the actual control, the corrected copy is not the original and the patch test is not degenerate. Codex demoted its own best answer because it accepted the framing.

2. Q3 and Q4 contradict each other and Codex does not notice. Q3 concedes "there is no independent answer key" for the control. Q4 then defines the cheapest honest measurement as "CONFIRM-only false positive rate = valid confirmed criticals against true claims / adjudicated criticals against true claims" — a formula whose numerator AND denominator both require per-claim truth labels the Run B control does not have. No deterministic mechanism for classifying an existing control claim as true is supplied anywhere. By Codex's own Q3 standard, its Q4 replay measurement is not computable; it is honest only on the machine-generated corpus it deferred to a later build.

3. Byte-range provenance is largely unbuildable as described. "byte ranges read if possible" and "did it read enough bytes to include the accused location" — a Python falsifier doing open(p).read() consumes the whole file, so the recorded span is [0, EOF] and the claim-span link is vacuous. The check collapses to file-open granularity, which Codex itself concedes at item 9 is "not enough". Ranked #3 as mandatory, it delivers less discrimination than the prose implies.

4. Item 9 (dynamic taint) is aspiration, not design. "For Python this is difficult but possible in constrained cases by wrapping file reads and parsed strings" is the entire mechanism. Wrapped strings do not survive int(), float(), regex captures, arithmetic, or C-level library calls — precisely the operations a numeric falsifier performs. It is listed as "the principled endpoint" with no account of how taint survives the transformations that matter.

5. Outcome-tuple extraction (item 4, the panel's likely favourite) is asserted, never specified. "unit", "operator", "tolerance" normalization across free-text technical prose is the hard part and gets no treatment. Whether the extractor is regex, a parser, or a model is left open — and if it is a model, the hard constraint is breached at the measurement step.

6. Cost labels are asserted, not derived. Rerun stability in "fresh sandboxes" is labelled cost "low" while multiplying every falsifier execution by N plus sandbox setup. Counterfactual patching is "medium" with no cost attached to generating patches over unstructured prose. The machine-generated corpus in Q3 — the largest single build in the response — carries no cost estimate at all, which matters because it is Codex's headline recommendation.

7. Q5 point 3 presents hypotheses in the position of evidence. Eight harms are listed ("affect the decay curve; delay convergence; consume expensive verification; pollute shared round context; bias later model attention; enter registries before adjudication; create human-review burden; mask true positives in noise") with no statement of which are observed in the archive, which are measurable, or which would be falsified by what. It hedges with "may still be a system defect if the pipeline treats candidate criticals as operationally meaningful before confirmation" without checking whether this pipeline does.

8. The phase-boundary trust relocation (see determinism field) is unflagged. For a response this careful about the hard constraint elsewhere, leaving the model-declared verdict block unexamined at rank #1 is a gap.

9. It accepts the repaired control revision as trustworthy — "Use only Run B, not Run A. Run A is contaminated by the earlier defective control revision" — while its Q3 answer says the document's correctness is an authorial assumption. Same inconsistency as point 2, showing up as an operational recommendation rather than a formula.

answers.verdict: YES as a blocking signal, but the criterion must be widened from "opened the file" to "causally bound to runner-authenticated claim material". Merely opening is insufficient; reading the whole file without using the accused span is insufficient; and there are legitimate falsifiers that need not open the document at all.
answers.quote:
A falsifier that **never reads the accused target passage, and is not otherwise given a runner-authenticated copy of that passage**, should not be allowed to close a critical finding. It may still be an interesting program, but it has not demonstrated that the named claim in the target document is defective.

The correct blocking rule is:

> A falsifier may close a finding only if its failure is causally tied to either  
> 1. bytes read from the accused target span, or  
> 2. a runner-provided canonical claim object containing the accused text, location, and hash.

Merely opening the file is not enough. Reading the whole file but never using the accused passage is not enough. Reading the accused passage and then failing because of an unrelated setup assertion is not enough. [...] So the strongest objection is valid: **“must open the target file” is too narrow.** [...] So: **open-the-target is sound as a blocking signal when absent, but only if “target” includes runner-authenticated claim material.**
answers.reasoning: It gives the concrete counterexample the question demanded (a falsifier testing `compute("case_42")` against the reference implementation, and a SHA-256 digest check) and then repairs the criterion rather than discarding it. Note the concrete code example has inverted assertion polarity — see weaknesses.

answers.verdict: Ten deterministic mechanisms, explicitly ranked; build order given as provenance classifier, claim binding, span-read logging, structured actual/expected outcomes, metamorphic repair reruns, archive signature quarantine, dynamic taint last. The single highest-value item is classifying failures by execution phase rather than by keyword.
answers.quote:
If money is tight, build in this order:

1. **Failure provenance classifier** — stops setup failures becoming confirmations.
2. **Target/canonical-claim binding** — requires real connection to accused claim.
3. **Span-read logging** — detects no-target and wrong-target falsifiers.
4. **Structured actual/expected outcome emission** — catches wrong-claim demonstrations.
5. **Metamorphic repair reruns** — strong when the finding names a concrete correction.
6. **Archive duplicate/error-signature quarantine** — cheap secondary filter.
7. **Dynamic taint** — powerful but later.
answers.reasoning: This is the most substantive answer in the response. The provenance item is stated in implementable terms: "run falsifier under a wrapper; record import phase, setup phase, check phase; require the failure signal to occur after target binding has succeeded; classify all pre-check failures as INVALID / UNTOOLABLE, never CONFIRMED." It also explicitly defends phase separation against the constraint: "This is not model adjudication. It is mechanical phase separation."

answers.verdict: The zero-plant control is the right KIND of instrument but is not sufficient as built, because its truth is an authorial assumption rather than a mechanical certification. Replace the hand-authored control with an oracle-generated corpus whose every claim is produced and hash-locked by an executable oracle, plus a paired planted version for sensitivity.
answers.quote:
A zero-plant control is useful, but not sufficient as described.

The weakness is exactly as stated: “all claims true” is not an answer key unless truth is mechanically certified. If the document is merely believed clean by its authors, then a confirmed critical against it could mean either:

1. the falsifier produced a false positive; or  
2. the authors missed a real defect. [...] So: a zero-plant control is the right **kind** of negative control only if its truth is certified by an external deterministic oracle. A hand-authored “believed clean” document is not strong enough.
answers.reasoning: This is where it lands the un-tampered-is-not-correct point. It also proposes the paired clean/planted design with the answer key "sealed from models and unavailable to falsifiers", yielding false-positive rate, true-positive rate and discrimination behaviour from one apparatus.

answers.verdict: Six minimum machinery items; then two experiment options. Cheapest if Run B prose is recoverable: deterministically re-extract falsifiers from archived raw responses, map to finding+claim, rerun on the hash-matching post-repair target, reclassify with the fixed verdict reader — no new five-model run. If not recoverable: ONE single round of the five-model panel against a small oracle-generated document, not a full convergence run. Report an explicit rule-of-three upper bound if zero confirmations.
answers.reasoning: The rule-of-three claim checks out: exact one-sided 95% bound 1 - 0.05^(1/n) gives 0.0950 at n=30 vs 3/n = 0.100, 0.0295 at n=100 vs 0.030 — 3/n is correct and slightly conservative, and it hedged with "rough". It also supplies a literal report template with separate denominators for candidates, serialized falsifiers and executable falsifiers. It correctly rules out the model-adjudication shortcut on the cheap path: "If humans or models have to guess which falsifier belongs to which finding, the result is contaminated."

answers.verdict: Accepts the steelman in PART and only in part. Concedes the terminology — candidate criticals are not measured false positives — but rejects the conclusion that only the section-4/2(c) mechanical faults are real, on four grounds: the decisive evidence path did not exist, the verdict classifier could convert setup failures into confirmations, the discrimination control is structurally degenerate on clean documents, and candidate criticals still have operational cost.
answers.quote:
I accept that reading only in part.

It is correct that **candidate criticals are not false positives under CONFIRM-only**. Calling them measured false positives would be wrong.

But I do not accept that there is no broader defect, for four reasons. [...] So the concept of CONFIRM-only is sound. The implementation, as measured, was not yet capable of honestly measuring its own false-positive rate.
answers.reasoning: Reason 2 is the sharpest: "This is worse than candidate noise. A setup assertion can become a false CONFIRMED result. That violates the core contract: > fail iff the named defect is real." Reason 3 concedes the design gap the prompt itself named, which is agreement rather than independent attack.

attacked_the_framing: Two attacks, one terminological and one methodological. (1) On the headline framing: "The framing is mostly right, but one term needs tightening: the measured "critical findings" in Runs A/B are not false positives under CONFIRM-only. They are **candidate critical accusations before adjudication**. The actual false-positive rate of the CONFIRM-only system is indeed unmeasured because the falsifier source was not serialized and the runs were interrupted." It then refuses to let that concession absolve the system: "That said, this is still a real defect in the review machinery, not merely an optics problem. A system whose safety boundary is "runnable falsifiers decide" must preserve, execute, and classify those falsifiers correctly." (2) On Q1's own criterion: it rejects "open the target file" as too narrow AND as too weak in the same breath — "Merely opening the file is not enough. Reading the whole file but never using the accused passage is not enough." (3) On the control instrument: it rejects the section-2 premise that a hand-authored document's claims are true by authorial intent — see false_premise_evidence. It does NOT attack gamma, the stopping rule, or the CONFIRM-only architecture itself; it endorses the concept.

concrete_proposals.name: Failure provenance classifier (phase-tagged execution wrapper)
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Runs each falsifier under a wrapper that records import phase, setup phase and check phase separately, and tags the failure by exception provenance rather than by keywords in the assertion message. Enumerated failure classes: "import/setup failure; target file not found; dependency missing; permission error; timeout; syntax error; assertion failure in the check phase; explicit FALSIFIED emitted in the check phase." "Only the last two should be eligible for CONFIRMED." "require the failure signal to occur after target binding has succeeded; classify all pre-check failures as INVALID / UNTOOLABLE, never CONFIRMED."
concrete_proposals.cost: low
concrete_proposals.catches: The section-4 keyword-classifier bug directly. Its example: an `AssertionError: target file exists` "must not be treated as proof of the accused defect. It is a setup failure." This is the strongest and most immediately buildable item in the response.

concrete_proposals.name: Target-span read coverage instrumentation
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Instruments file reads and records whether the falsifier opened the target and whether it read bytes overlapping the accused claim span; better version asks whether the span was read BEFORE the failure signal, whether only metadata was read, and whether the wrong path was read.
concrete_proposals.cost: low to medium
concrete_proposals.catches: Falsifiers that never inspect the accused material. HOSTILE NOTE: as specified this degenerates to trivially-true for any falsifier that does `open(target).read()`, which is the common shape. ChatGPT states the requirement it cannot meet ("Reading the whole file but never using the accused passage is not enough") but the only proposal that would actually meet it is dynamic taint, which it ranks last and defers.

concrete_proposals.name: Canonical claim binding object
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: The runner extracts the accused claim as structured data and passes it to the falsifier: {claim_id, target_path, start_byte, end_byte, claim_text, claim_hash}. A falsifier may then either read the target itself or consume this object; "If it uses neither, it cannot close the finding."
concrete_proposals.cost: medium
concrete_proposals.catches: Hard-coded model paraphrases of the claim, and rescues legitimate falsifiers that test an executable claim without reopening the document. HOSTILE NOTE: the extraction step — how a free-text model finding is mapped to a byte span in the target — is never specified. This is the load-bearing unbuilt piece; if it were done by a model it would violate the hard constraint, and ChatGPT does not say how it is done.

concrete_proposals.name: Path-resolution and staging checks
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Records "every attempted path open; whether the path exists; whether it is inside the staged target directory; whether the path points to the actual target; whether the failure occurred before any target read."
concrete_proposals.cost: low
concrete_proposals.catches: Mis-pathed falsifiers, which the prompt says is the ordinary failure mode because controls are staged outside the repo. "A falsifier that dies because `Path("docs/control.md").exists()` is false has demonstrated nothing about the target document."

concrete_proposals.name: Explicit setup/check protocol (bench.falsifier_api)
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Falsifiers must call `setup_ok()` after setup and `confirm_defect("structured reason")` on defect detection. "The runner then only treats `confirm_defect(...)` or a post-`setup_ok()` `AssertionError` as eligible failure signals."
concrete_proposals.cost: medium
concrete_proposals.catches: Setup failures masquerading as defect demonstrations. Its own defence of the constraint: "This is not model adjudication. It is mechanical phase separation." HOSTILE NOTE: depends on model compliance with a new emission format; no compliance rate estimated, and no policy stated for non-compliant but legitimate falsifiers.

concrete_proposals.name: Structured actual/expected outcome emission and comparison
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Falsifier emits {claimed, computed, operator, units}; runner compares those numbers against runner-extracted values from the accused claim and from the finding prose, plus units, variable names, equation identifiers and table labels.
concrete_proposals.cost: low to medium
concrete_proposals.catches: "falsifiers proving the wrong thing" — prose accuses one constant, falsifier fails on a different one. HOSTILE NOTE: checks internal coherence between finding and falsifier only; it cannot distinguish a true finding from a false one. "match" is undefined for floats/units. Fallback on no-match is "route to human review", which is HIL cost, not computation.

concrete_proposals.name: Metamorphic accused-span repair
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Build a patched copy of the target in which only the accused value is changed to the finding's stated correction, rerun the falsifier, and require: "fails on original; exits cleanly on patched copy. If it still fails, it probably is not testing the named defect."
concrete_proposals.cost: medium
concrete_proposals.catches: Falsifiers insensitive to the named defect. ★ HOSTILE FINDING — THIS PROPOSAL IS BROKEN ON EXACTLY THE CASE UNDER STUDY. On a clean document, a false-positive falsifier that hard-codes the finding's wrong "correct value" PASSES this test. Worked example using ChatGPT's own numbers: claim "The total is 143" is true; a false finding says "should be 134"; a falsifier asserting total == 134 fails on the original (recorded CONFIRMED) and exits cleanly on the 134-patched copy — scoring as a genuine defect demonstration. The check measures whether the falsifier agrees with its own finding, not whether the finding is true. ChatGPT gestures at a limit ("It does not work on a clean document unless the finding itself gives a concrete alternative outcome") but the "unless" clause is precisely backwards: when the finding does give a concrete alternative, the test actively launders the false positive.

concrete_proposals.name: Unrelated-span perturbation
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Change an unrelated passage, rerun, and require the verdict not to change.
concrete_proposals.cost: medium
concrete_proposals.catches: Whole-document, regex-fragile or line-number-dependent falsifiers. HOSTILE NOTE: the routing rule is not computable as written — "This should usually produce SUSPICION / UNTOOLABLE, not automatic REFUTED, because some document-wide claims are legitimate." "Usually" and "some claims are legitimate" require a judgement the response never mechanises.

concrete_proposals.name: Dynamic taint from target bytes to failure branch
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Propagate taint from reads of the accused span through execution to the branch that raises AssertionError or prints FALSIFIED; "Confirmed only if the failure branch is data-dependent on the accused span or canonical claim object."
concrete_proposals.cost: high
concrete_proposals.catches: "the deepest version of 'opened but did not use'". Self-deferred: "This is strong, but expensive and brittle in Python. I would not build it first." This honesty is creditable, but it means the one mechanism that would actually enforce its own Q1 criterion is the one it declines to build.

concrete_proposals.name: Archive duplicate/error-signature quarantine
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Across the 8500+ archived findings, detect repeated tracebacks, missing paths, assertion messages, stdout/stderr, identical falsifier bodies under different prose accusations, and repeated pre-target-read failures.
concrete_proposals.cost: low
concrete_proposals.catches: Broken falsifier templates reused across unrelated findings. Correctly scoped: "This does not prove an individual finding false, but it is a deterministic quarantine signal. A falsifier matching a known setup-failure signature should not be allowed to CONFIRM."

concrete_proposals.name: Oracle-generated clean corpus (replacement negative control)
concrete_proposals.what_it_computes: Generate every document claim from an executable oracle whose output is stored and hash-locked (function returns, determinants, SHA-256 digests, sorted outputs), render the target document FROM the oracle output, and hold a paired planted version with a sealed answer key.
concrete_proposals.cost: medium (one-off corpus build)
concrete_proposals.catches: Yields, from one apparatus: "false-positive rate on true claims; true-positive rate on planted false claims; discrimination behavior on repaired copies; end-to-end test of CONFIRM-only." This is the response's answer to both Q3 and Q4 and is its most consequential structural recommendation.

false_premise_evidence:
SPOTTED — stated explicitly, in its own words, in the Q3 answer:

"The weakness is exactly as stated: “all claims true” is not an answer key unless truth is mechanically certified. If the document is merely believed clean by its authors, then a confirmed critical against it could mean either:

1. the falsifier produced a false positive; or  
2. the authors missed a real defect."

and, as the design conclusion:

"So: a zero-plant control is the right **kind** of negative control only if its truth is certified by an external deterministic oracle. A hand-authored “believed clean” document is not strong enough."

and in the Q4 minimum-work list, as a required item rather than an aside:

"6. **Run against a deterministic oracle-clean target.**  
   Not merely an author-believed clean target."

It also draws the correct methodological consequence unprompted — its decisive falsification experiment requires an ORACLE-clean target precisely because a believed-clean one cannot support the inference: "1. build an oracle-clean target whose claims are mechanically true; 2. run the fixed system with falsifier serialization, fixed verdict classification, and target/canonical-claim binding; 3. obtain even one runner-CONFIRMED critical against a claim the oracle proves true."

TWO HONESTY CAVEATS AGAINST OVER-CREDITING. (a) The prompt's Q3 handed it the opening verbatim ("It has no answer key and the 'all claims true' property is itself an assumption made by its authors"), and ChatGPT opens by conceding exactly that: "The weakness is exactly as stated". So this is endorsement-plus-development of a premise the question already contained, not an unprompted discovery. (b) The one piece of empirical support it offers — "Run A already demonstrates this problem: seven claims were later repaired, so some “false positives” may have been true findings" — was also given in the prompt at section 2(b), so it is a restatement, not a new measurement. What it DOES add on its own: it generalises the point from Run A's pre-repair revision to the current post-repair document ("A hand-authored 'believed clean' document is not strong enough"), which is the actual gap, and it makes oracle-certification a blocking requirement for any honest false-positive measurement. That is well past a vague "the control may be imperfect" and clears the bar. It does NOT go the last step of saying the post-repair control probably still contains real defects, nor does it name any candidate defect class; it treats it as an epistemic possibility to be closed by construction, not as a live suspicion to be measured.
headline: ChatGPT (GPT-5.5 via OpenRouter, 140 s, 20118 chars) says the framing is right in substance but wrong in one word — the criticals against the control are "candidate critical accusations before adjudication", not measured false positives, and the CONFIRM-only false-positive rate "HAS NEVER ACTUALLY BEEN MEASURED". It accepts the Q5 steelman only in part: the concept is sound, the implementation was not capable of measuring itself. Its constructive core is to widen open-the-target into "bound to the accused claim by a deterministic, runner-verifiable data path", to classify falsifier failures by execution phase rather than keyword, and to replace the hand-authored zero-plant control with an oracle-generated corpus whose truth is hash-locked rather than believed.
strongest_falsification:
Verbatim, its designated strongest falsification of the position it expects others to take:

"I expect some reviewers to say:

> “Once serialization and the keyword classifier are fixed, there is no substantive defect. The noisy criticals are harmless because CONFIRM-only will filter them.”

The strongest deterministic falsification would be:

1. build an oracle-clean target whose claims are mechanically true;
2. run the fixed system with falsifier serialization, fixed verdict classification, and target/canonical-claim binding;
3. obtain even one runner-CONFIRMED critical against a claim the oracle proves true.

That single case would refute the claim that the remaining issue was merely logging or setup-failure classification. It would show that CONFIRM-only can still close a false critical under clean deterministic conditions."

ASSESSMENT: it is a well-posed decisive experiment with a single-instance refutation criterion, which is the right shape. But it is not an attack on any other model's reasoning — it is a restatement of its own Q4 answer pointed at a hypothetical opponent, and it is unfalsifiable in the near term by construction ("Until that experiment is run, the honest verdict is..."). Its genuinely sharper attack sits elsewhere, in Q5 reason 2: "This is worse than candidate noise. A setup assertion can become a false CONFIRMED result. That violates the core contract: > fail iff the named defect is real. A falsifier that fails because the target path is wrong has not demonstrated the defect."
violates_determinism_constraint:
No outright violation — nothing in the response resolves a finding by model vote, model verdict or model confidence, and it twice guards the boundary explicitly ("This is not model adjudication. It is mechanical phase separation."; "If humans or models have to guess which falsifier belongs to which finding, the result is contaminated."). Four places where determinism is claimed but not delivered:

1. UNSPECIFIED CLAIM EXTRACTION — the biggest exposure. Proposals 3 and 6 both rest on "a runner-provided canonical claim object", "runner-extracted claim text", "a runner-extracted value from the accused claim". The mechanism that maps a free-text model finding to {target_path, start_byte, end_byte, claim_text, claim_hash} is never described. If that mapping is performed by a model, the hard constraint is violated at the foundation of the two central proposals; if by the model emitting its own byte offsets, that is model-asserted data the runner can only hash-verify for existence, not for relevance. ChatGPT does not address this at all.

2. HUMAN-REVIEW ESCAPE HATCH — proposal 6: "No match: route to human review or INVALID, not CONFIRMED." Permitted under the letter of the constraint (HIL is not model adjudication) but it is not computation, and no bound is given on how often it fires. Given this project's standing HIL-fatigue concern, an unbounded human-review route is a cost, not a solution.

3. NON-COMPUTABLE ROUTING IN PROPOSAL 8 — "This should usually produce SUSPICION / UNTOOLABLE, not automatic REFUTED, because some document-wide claims are legitimate." "Usually" and "some ... are legitimate" name a judgement with no decision procedure attached.

4. MODEL-SUPPLIED PATCH VALUE IN PROPOSAL 7 — the metamorphic repair patches the document with the correction the FINDING asserts. Not model adjudication of the verdict, but the discrimination signal is driven entirely by model-authored content, and on a clean document that inverts the test (see concrete_proposals entry 7).
weaknesses:
★ 1. THE ONE CONCRETE FALSIFIER IT WRITES HAS INVERTED POLARITY. Q1's headline counterexample is:

  Target claim: "The reference implementation returns 17 for input `case_42`."
  Falsifier: `assert compute("case_42") != 17`

Under the contract the prompt states — fail (raise AssertionError) if and only if the defect is real — this is backwards. If the defect is real, compute returns something other than 17, the assertion HOLDS, and the falsifier exits cleanly. It raises exactly when the document's claim is TRUE. The one piece of executable code offered as a model of a legitimate falsifier is a falsifier that confirms the defect when there is none. In a panel review about telling true findings from false ones, this is not a typo-level slip.

★ 2. PROPOSAL 7 (METAMORPHIC REPAIR) LAUNDERS FALSE POSITIVES ON CLEAN DOCUMENTS. Full derivation in the concrete_proposals entry. Short form: a falsifier that hard-codes the finding's wrong "correct value" fails on the original and passes on the patched copy, scoring as a genuine defect demonstration. ChatGPT calls this "the discrimination control, but generalized" — it inherits the degeneracy it was meant to repair, and its stated limit clause ("does not work on a clean document unless the finding itself gives a concrete alternative outcome") has the condition exactly reversed.

3. PROPOSAL 2 CANNOT ENFORCE THE CRITERION PROPOSAL 1 ESTABLISHES. Q1 rules that "Reading the whole file but never using the accused passage is not enough". Proposal 2's minimum version asks only "Did it read bytes overlapping the accused claim span?" — trivially satisfied by `open(target).read()`, the most common falsifier idiom. The only proposal that closes the gap is dynamic taint (9), which it ranks last and declines to build. So the ranked build order does not, at any point in its own sequence, deliver the Q1 criterion.

4. "RUNNER-EXTRACTED" IS DOING ENORMOUS UNEXAMINED WORK. See violates_determinism_constraint item 1. Two of its top four ranked proposals depend on a claim-extraction step it never specifies.

5. OUTCOME MATCHING IS UNDER-SPECIFIED WHERE IT MATTERS. "at least one side must match a runner-extracted value" — no float tolerance, no normalisation across notations (0.031 vs 3.1e-2 vs 3.1%), no unit reconciliation, no policy for derived values that differ in the last digit. It also lists "variable names; equation identifiers; table row / column labels" as comparable fields without any extraction method for prose documents.

6. Q4 ITEM 1 IS A NO-OP. Its "minimum required machinery" list opens with "Serialize falsifier source into each finding record. Already fixed today, according to the prompt." Padding the minimum-work list with work the prompt says is already done inflates the apparent answer.

7. THE CHEAP EXPERIMENT MAY NOT EXIST. Its no-new-run path requires "If the archived Run B raw model responses contain unambiguous finding IDs and falsifier blocks" — but section 2(c) says the falsifiers appeared only as prose mentions, never as serialised records. It flags the risk honestly ("But it only works if the mapping is unambiguous") yet proposes no deterministic mapping test and no way to report the unmappable fraction as an explicit denominator, so the reader cannot tell in advance whether the cheap path is available at all.

8. THE "STRONGEST FALSIFICATION" IS ITS OWN Q4 ANSWER RE-AIMED. It attacks a hypothetical opponent position rather than any specific competing reasoning, and terminates in a holding statement ("Until that experiment is run, the honest verdict is...") rather than a claim that could be checked today.

9. NO ENGAGEMENT WITH COST OR SCALE. Cost labels are qualitative only — "low", "medium", "high" — with no engineering estimate, no throughput figure, and no statement of what fraction of the archived 8500+ findings each check would be computable on. The prompt supplied two such coverage figures (32% and 20%) and ChatGPT never uses either, nor predicts what its own proposals would achieve.

10. CREDIT WHERE DUE, TO KEEP THE LEDGER HONEST: the failure-provenance classifier (proposal 1) is specified tightly enough to build from the text as written; the rule-of-three bound at n=30 gives 0.100 against an exact 1-0.05^(1/n) = 0.0950, so "about 3/n" is correct and appropriately hedged; the report template with separate denominators (candidates / serialized / executable) is the single most useful concrete artefact in the response; and the Q5 partial-acceptance is genuinely reasoned rather than split-the-difference.

answers.verdict: REJECTS it as a blocking criterion. Calls it "a useful heuristic but unsound as a strict blocking criterion" — it wrongly refuses pure-logic refutations of derived claims, and `import` may not register as an explicit `open()` in a naive check.
answers.quote: The "open-the-target" check is a useful heuristic but **unsound as a strict blocking criterion**. It correctly catches falsifiers that test a hallucinated mock rather than the real artefact, but it wrongly refuses a critical class of legitimate falsifiers: **pure-logic refutations of derived claims.** [...] If the runner blocks this because `open(target)` was never called, it rejects a mathematically sound proof of a defect. Furthermore, if the target is a code module, the falsifier interacts with it via `import`, which triggers OS-level reads but may not register as an explicit `open()` call in a naive static analysis or monkey-patched `builtins.open` check.
answers.reasoning: Its headline case AGAINST is self-defeating on inspection. The Equation-3 example hardcodes `500` and `params` into the falsifier — those values reach the falsifier only by transcription from the target, and an unverified transcription is exactly the hallucination class the criterion exists to catch. So its strongest argument against the check is arguably the check's strongest argument for. The second point (importlib uses `_io.open_code`, not `builtins.open`, so a monkey-patched-open detector misses imports) is a genuine, correct, mechanically actionable implementation caveat and the more valuable half of the answer.

answers.verdict: Two ranked mechanisms plus the sub-question. (1) Strict exception typing — ONLY `AssertionError` (or a clean-exit stdout token) counts as CONFIRMED; every other exception class is deterministically INVALID_FALSIFIER/REFUTED. (2) Target execution coverage under coverage.py or sys.settrace; zero lines of the target executed means it tested a mock. Both deterministic. It supplied only two, against a question asking for a ranked list.
answers.quote:
**1. Strict Exception Typing (Cost: Trivial | Catch: Massive)**
*   **Mechanism:** The runner must ONLY accept `AssertionError` (or a clean exit with a specific stdout token like `FALSIFIED`) as a CONFIRMED verdict. Any `FileNotFoundError`, `ImportError`, `NameError`, or `TypeError` is deterministically classified as an INVALID_FALSIFIER (Refuted).
answers.reasoning:
Three defects. (a) It collapses INVALID into REFUTED — "INVALID_FALSIFIER (Refuted)", and in Q4 "Anything else = REFUTED". A falsifier that dies in setup establishes nothing about the claim; recording REFUTED asserts the claim survived a test it never received. That converts a measurement failure into a positive result — this project's named governing failure mode. (b) A large class of genuine defects manifests AS an uncaught exception in the target. On this very control document, "the hash ring mis-routes exact matches" could surface as an IndexError/KeyError raised inside the target — Gemini's rule classifies that demonstration as INVALID and then as REFUTED. Concrete false negative. (c) The `stdout token like FALSIFIED` escape hatch reintroduces substring matching — the exact defect Gemini says this proposal eliminates ("This immediately eliminates the keyword-parsing bug in Section 4"), and the exact shape of this project's recorded loss where a reader matched `NOT FALSIFIED` as containing `FALSIFIED`. It is self-undermining in the same sentence.

On coverage: the bar it states is wrong. "If coverage > 0 and it raises `AssertionError`, it actually exercised the target" is false — importing a module executes its top-level lines and yields coverage > 0 with nothing exercised. The check needs coverage of the specific functions/lines named in the finding, which Gemini does not say. Scope mismatch too: Q1 explicitly contemplates prose targets ("If a target document claims..."), but "line coverage of the target module" is undefined for a Markdown design document, which is what the control actually is.

answers.verdict: Zero-plant is the right instrument — "mathematically correct and necessary" — but the implementation is flawed because its correctness is authorial assumption, not mechanical guarantee. Remedy: replace the prose document with a formally verified algorithm (Python translation of a proven Coq/Lean snippet) or a trivially exhaustive state machine.
answers.quote: A zero-plant control is the **mathematically correct and necessary instrument** for measuring False Positive Rate (FPR), because FPR requires a denominator of true negatives. [...] However, the *implementation* of the control is flawed because "all claims true" is an authorial assumption, not a mechanical guarantee. [...] A **Mechanically Verified Zero-Plant Control**. Instead of a prose technical document, the target should be a formally verified algorithm (e.g., a Python translation of a proven Coq/Lean snippet) [...] In this target, correctness is not assumed; it is mathematically guaranteed. Any critical finding against it is, by definition, a false positive.
answers.reasoning: This is the best paragraph in the response and it carries the false-premise catch (see below). Two overclaims. "Necessary" is wrong: a fully audited document with a per-claim answer key supplies both FP and TN denominators without being zero-plant — its own remedy is in fact an answer-key control, not a zero-plant one. And the remedy re-opens the gap it closes: "a Python translation of a proven Coq/Lean snippet" means the verified object is the Coq/Lean, and the unverified translation is what the panel attacks. "By definition" also overclaims — a finding can attack the specification the proof is relative to, which is a true positive against the artefact as delivered.

answers.verdict: Patch the runner with strict exception typing, then run ONE model for ONE round against the post-repair control, count criticals, run their falsifiers, and take the CONFIRMED count as "your exact False Positive count". Cost: one API call sequence, zero human adjudication.
answers.quote: If the model generates 15 criticals, and the runner refutes all 15 because they throw `NameError` or exit cleanly, your CONFIRM-only FPR is 0%. Cost: One API call sequence, zero human adjudication.
answers.reasoning: The measurement step is stated as "**Result:** The number of CONFIRMED findings is your exact False Positive count." That is the false premise re-encoded as a procedure, and it directly contradicts the Q3 paragraph written moments earlier. The charitable reading is that "post-repair zero-plant control" means Q3's formally verified target, in which case the identity holds — but Gemini never says so and never retracts the general form. Separately: n=1 model, n=1 round yields a point count with no confidence interval and cannot "settle" a rate; and it never names the denominator (it is inferable as criticals-emitted only from the 15/15 worked example). It also declares historical data useless for this metric because of the serialization bug and the flawed exception handler, which is a sound and useful call.

answers.verdict: ACCEPTS the steelman without reservation. The panel is a fuzzer/Generator, the runner is the Discriminator; generating 29 criticals on a clean document is intended behaviour, and the only real defects are the serialization bug and the keyword-parser bug. Fix the Discriminator and the system works as designed.
answers.quote:
**Verdict: I accept this reading entirely.**
The premise of the `CONFIRM-only` architecture is that LLM prose is inherently untrustworthy and prone to hallucination. If we expected the LLM to have a 0% false-positive rate on its own, we wouldn't have built the mechanical falsifier loop. Penalizing the LLM for generating false positives on a clean document is a category error; it is blaming the fuzzer for generating bad inputs. Fix the Discriminator (the runner's exception handling), and the system works as designed.
answers.reasoning: The question was "Accept or reject, and exactly where it fails?" Gemini answered the first half and refused the second — it names no failure point in the steelman at all. That is evasion of an explicitly asked sub-question, and it matters because the obvious failure point undercuts its own architecture: if CONFIRM-only is the sole precision mechanism, the Discriminator's soundness is load-bearing, and the entire episode is evidence that the Discriminator was not sound. "Fix the Discriminator ... and the system works as designed" is asserted, never falsified. It also twice calls the target "a clean document" — reverting to the premise it questioned in Q3.

attacked_the_framing: Three ways. (1) It rejected Q1's implicit premise that the open-the-target check is soundly blocking, downgrading it to \"a useful heuristic\". (2) It reframed the entire problem as a Generator-Discriminator architecture in which LLM false positives are not a defect but the intended output of a fuzzer: \"If an LLM generates 29 critical findings on a clean document, it is functioning exactly as an adversarial fuzzer should. The fact that these candidates exist is not a defect; it is the intended behavior of the Generator.\" (3) Unprompted, it appended a section titled \"Falsification of the Expected Panel Position\" in which it invents a position it predicts the other panel models will hold — \"complex prompt-engineering, 'self-reflection' loops, or multi-agent debate\" — and falsifies that. Nobody stated that position. It is attacking a straw panel, though the argument it makes against it is substantive. Also worth recording as framing: it questioned the control's epistemic status in Q3 and then reverted to calling the same document \"clean\" in Q4 and Q5.
computed_outcome_view:
Yes, emphatically, and on explicit no-model-adjudication grounds — but framed principally as a DEDUPLICATION mechanism rather than as a discriminator between "demonstrates the named defect" and "fails for an unrelated reason", which was the question asked. Verbatim: "**3. Sub-question: Comparing Computed Outcomes (Cost: Low | Catch: High for Deduplication)**
*   **Mechanism:** Mandate that falsifiers write a structured artifact (e.g., `verdict.json`) containing the computed constants: `{"expected": X, "actual": Y}`. 
*   **Why:** Comparing prose is fuzzy and requires LLMs. Comparing `{"actual": 404}` from Finding A and `{"actual": 404}` from Finding B is a deterministic, O(1) equality check. If two falsifiers produce the exact same computed deviation, they are duplicates. If they produce different deviations, they are distinct failure modes. This is highly discriminating and entirely mechanical."

Hostile note: both halves of the biconditional are false as stated. Two independent defects routinely produce the same computed deviation (collisions on 0, 1, None, empty, and 404-style sentinels will be common), so identical outcome does not imply duplicate; and one defect produces different deviations under different inputs, so different outcome does not imply distinct failure mode. No float tolerance is specified, so exact equality on derived floats is brittle in both directions. And nothing binds the `expected` field to the target document — a falsifier built on a hallucinated constant writes its hallucination into `expected` and the comparison happily proceeds. So the mechanism is real, cheap and genuinely deterministic, but it is a grouping heuristic presented with the language of a proof ("O(1)", "entirely mechanical", "highly discriminating").

concrete_proposals.catches: Falsifiers that never touch the real artefact. answers.verdict: REJECT the steelman, on two grounds that survive fixing every implementation bug: (1) the termination logic can loop forever because an unbounded adversarial search keeps emitting NEW candidate criticals on a clean document; (2) the corrected-copy discrimination control is structurally blind when the document is clean, because the 'corrected copy' is the original.
answers.quote: **Do I accept this reading?** **No.** I reject it on two design-ground failures that persist even after the mechanical bugs are fixed. 1. **Termination logic is vulnerable to persistent false positives.** The system stops when a decay-curve on critical findings flattens *and* K consecutive rounds produce no new criticals. On a clean document, a panel instructed to find problems will continue to generate *new* candidate criticals because it is an unbounded adversarial search. Even if most are filtered by CONFIRM-only, they remain *new findings* in the panel's output, so the "no new criticals" condition may never be met. The system can loop indefinitely. That is a termination defect, not an implementation bug; it stems from the assumption that false positives will eventually exhaust themselves, which they won't on a document with no real weaknesses. 2. **The discrimination control is structurally blind when the document is clean.** The control relies on a corrected copy of the target where the claimed defect is fixed. If the document has no defects, the "corrected copy" is the original itself, so the control never fires.

Point 1 is asserted with zero evidence, no bound, and no computation — it is a claim about model behaviour presented as a design proof, and it directly contradicts this project's standing position that non-convergence is mechanical rather than model-driven. Preserved here as genuine disagreement, not smoothed. Note also that DeepSeek makes the corrected-copy control the centrepiece of point 2 without ever asking who PRODUCES the corrected copy — if a model does, that is model adjudication sitting inside the architecture it is defending, and DeepSeek misses it entirely.

headline: DeepSeek rejects both the instrument and the steelman: the zero-plant control has no ground truth and cannot ever have one, so the false-positive rate has never been measured and cannot be measured by filters alone. It offers four cheap deterministic filters (only one of which is actually buildable as specified), a log-replay experiment that reuses already-paid-for runs, and a planted-defect benchmark whose own scoring rule reproduces the exact fallacy DeepSeek had just identified.

violates_determinism_constraint: No explicit violation — DeepSeek never proposes voting, confidence scores, or model adjudication, and it is constraint-aware enough to reject further filters on exactly those grounds ("any check beyond (1)-(4) that tries to infer intent will quickly need a model in the loop, violating the hard constraint"). DeepSeek's disposition for a finding that fails the open-the-target check is "the finding is not discarded; it is sent to human review". Human review is HIL, which this project permits for confirmation, but it is not computable by the runner — DeepSeek's answer to Q1 therefore resolves the hard case by exiting the constraint rather than satisfying it, and it does not acknowledge doing so. (2) Q2(4) UNSPECIFIED SEMANTIC STEP: "For free-text, a lightweight syntactic comparison can catch repeats or near-contradictions." Near-contradiction detection over free text has no deterministic implementation; any real build reaches for embeddings or a model, at which point the constraint is broken. DeepSeek gives no algorithm, so the violation is latent rather than committed — but this is precisely where it would land. (3) Q5 UNSPECIFIED PRODUCER: DeepSeek builds its second and best objection on the corrected-copy discrimination control and proposes "executing the corrected-copy mechanism with a manufactured defect", without once asking who authors the corrected copy or the manufactured defect. If a model does, adjudication is already inside the architecture DeepSeek is critiquing, and it misses this entirely while treating that same control as the thing that would rescue the design.

SELF-CONTRADICTION, Q3, THE MOST SERIOUS. Having falsified the zero-plant control with the Run A seven-corrections example, DeepSeek prescribes a planted-defect benchmark scored by "If a finding points to a planted defect, it is a true positive; otherwise it is a false positive." That rule assumes the unplanted remainder is correct — the identical un-tampered-equals-correct fallacy it had just demolished. Its replacement instrument carries the confound it was built to remove, and DeepSeek never notices.

NOT COMPUTABLE AS WRITTEN, Q2(2). "run the falsifier with a coverage tool (e.g., coverage.py on a Python harness that opens the target file). If none of the lines in the claim's region are ever executed" — coverage.py measures executed lines of Python source. The lines of a prose/markdown target document are data and are never executed, so document-line coverage does not exist as described. The buildable version is a traced file-read wrapper recording consumed byte ranges; DeepSeek does not describe it, and its "a few dozen lines of scripting" estimate is for a thing that cannot be written. This is the response's clearest instance of rigorous-sounding prose that dissolves on inspection, and it is ranked SECOND in its own priority list.

REPRODUCES THE PROJECT'S KNOWN DEFECT, Q2(1). The valid-verdict rule includes "printed the token `FALSIFIED`". UNCHECKED DEPENDENCIES, Q4. The whole experiment rests on falsifier code existing in the transcripts as fenced blocks labelled `FALSIFIER:` "(or similar patterns)" — an unverified assumption about the log format that DeepSeek does not flag as a risk, and if false the proposal is worth nothing. Claim mapping is by "searching for claim IDs in surrounding text", a proximity heuristic that will mis-map silently, which is this project's governing failure mode rendered as a build step.

ASSERTION WITHOUT EVIDENCE, Q5(1). The non-termination argument — "a panel instructed to find problems will continue to generate *new* candidate criticals because it is an unbounded adversarial search ... The system can loop indefinitely" — carries no bound, no measurement, no computation, and no engagement with any observed convergence. It is a claim about model behaviour presented in the register of a design proof, and it contradicts this project's standing position that non-convergence is mechanical. Preserved as real disagreement, but recorded as unevidenced.

MISSED THE OBVIOUS ADJUDICATION LEAK, Q5(2). DeepSeek makes the corrected-copy control central to its best objection without ever asking who produces the corrected copy. That is the one place model adjudication most plausibly already sits in the architecture, and the response walks past it.

COST RANKING IS NOT A COST RANKING, Q2.
